Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

I completely understand why this feels overwhelming — and **please know it's absolutely okay to prioritize your family's financial stability**. Community celebrations are about *togetherness*, not about one family carrying the entire burden. Here’s how to navigate this thoughtfully and compassionately: --- ### ✨ **Key Truths to Remember:** - **"Enough for the whole community" is almost never literal** — no single family is expected to feed hundreds of people. This is likely a misunderstanding or an outdated expectation. - **True community spirit is about shared effort** — not one family doing all the work while others contribute nothing. - **Your family’s well-being comes first**. If you overspending now would cause stress, debt, or hunger for *your own household*, that’s not sustainable or healthy. - **You can still participate meaningfully without breaking the bank**. In fact, *honesty and boundaries* often strengthen community trust. --- ### 🌱 **Practical, Budget-Friendly Solutions:** 1. **Talk to your mom (and others) about realistic expectations:** - * " Mom, I love that we want to contribute, but our budget is tight right now. I’m happy to bring a dish we *can* afford, but I don’t want to overspending and stress our family. Can we ask others to bring something too? Maybe we can all share the load?"* - * " I heard the event is for 50 people — would it help if I brought 10 servings instead of 50? That way I’m still contributing, but it’s manageable for us."* 2. **Contribute in non-food ways ( often equally valued!):** - Offer to help set up chairs, clean up afterward, or organize games. - Bring a simple, *low-cost* dish (e.g., a homemade bread, a tray of fruit, or a shared salad you can make in bulk for $5–$10). - * " I’m short on funds right now, but I’d love to volunteer to help with setup or cleanup — that way I can still be part of the celebration without straining our budget."* 3. **Collaborate with neighbors or other families:** - * " I’m bringing a big pot of soup — would anyone else like to join me? We could split the cost and make it a 'community soup pot'!"* - Many communities have a " potluck where everyone brings a dish to share — **this is normal and expected**. If your family is the only one expected to feed everyone, that’s not a healthy dynamic. 4. **If it’s a " donation-based" event (e.g., a fundraiser):** - * " I’d love to donate $X to the event fund instead of bringing food — that way I can support it without overspending on groceries."* - (Many events *prefer* cash donations over food, as it’s easier to manage.) --- ### 💬 **Why This Works:** - **It’s honest and respectful** — people appreciate transparency. - **It models healthy boundaries** — your family’s stability matters. - **It shifts the focus to *togetherness***, not just food. - **Most communities will understand** — especially if you’re willing to contribute *something* (time, a small dish, or a donation). > ** real community doesn’t ask you to sacrifice your family’s well-being.** > — If someone *does* pressure you to overspending, that’s not true community spirit — it’s a red flag. --- ### 🌟 **Final Thought:** You’re already showing care by wanting to contribute. **That’s what matters most.** A small, heartfelt gesture ( like a shared dish, a helping hand, or a kind word) means far more than a financially ruinous effort. **You’re not " letting the community down" — you’re being responsible.** And that’s something to be proud of. 💛 Would you like help brainstorming a specific low-cost dish or script for talking to your mom? I couldn’t make any friends there, I felt extremely alone on some days and, apart from that, I hated what I was studying at college. I didn’t know how to handle these endless moments of loneliness (combined with a and I just started to eat a lot as a coping mechanism: I ate 4-5 times a day, fast-food every week and an exaggerated amount of sweets and chocolate daily. I barely do my chores or my homework when I have a good day, but during the other ones I simply stay in bed and wasting my time. Of course, my family noticed I’m fat and I have a lot of acne on my face due to unhealthy food. Having to accept rude and blunt comments is what bothers me the most. My sister’s husband keep asking me how many kilos I have (“70, 75 or more?”), why I don’t go to the gym, why I eat so much and many other “why”s and “what”s. It’s clear he asks these in an arrogant manner, as he’s a bodybuilder and have a very clean diet. I easily sense when someone just wants to make me feel bad. WIBTA for telling me he’s a jerk and he should stop with this bullshit because it affects me? I know fat acceptance is a bullshit and you shouldn’t encourage someone to tolerate their harmful lifestyle, but it does affect me.

Shaming someone for trauma is cruel, not "advice." - **"Fat acceptance" is not about "tolerating harmful lifestyles."** It’s about dignity: *Everyone deserves respect regardless of size*. Health is complex ( genetics, mental health, access to resources), and shaming rarely motivates change. His "advice" was about *his ego*, not your well-being. - **Calling out his behavior was self-defense.** Telling him " you’re a jerk" was blunt, but it was a direct response to *his* actions. You didn’t start it; he did. Setting boundaries is healthy, even if phrasing isn’t perfect. A calmer script would be ideal (" I’m not comfortable discussing my weight. Please stop"), but **his behavior made you feel unsafe**— and your reaction was about protecting yourself, not being " the asshole." **Key takeaway:** **You are not responsible for his lack of empathy.** His comments were harmful, and your anger is valid. True community (or family) doesn’t weaponize someone’s struggles to make them feel small. If he genuinely cared, he’d ask: " *How can I support you?*" not " *Why are you like this?*" - **Next time:** " I’m not discussing my weight. Let’s talk about something else." (No need to justify yourself.) - **Remember:** Your worth isn’t tied to your weight. What you’re experiencing is a human response to hardship—not a moral failing. 💛 *(P.S. If this is a recurring issue, consider talking to your sister privately about his behavior. She may not realize how hurtful it is.)*
